newsitem.title: USA: TIN - Industry braced for shootout with rivals.
newsitem.headline: TIN - Industry braced for shootout with rivals.

text.p: Shotgun cartridges, lead-free solder and a greater share of the beverage can market will combine to boost global tin consumption by 20,000 to 25,000 annually in 1997 compared to just two years ago, the International Tin Research Institute said.

"If continued growth is maintained to absorb future growth in production, then we have a stable price," Rod Bedder, ITRI's managing director, told the fall meeting of the American Tin Trade Association in New York on Thursday evening.
Taking 1994 as a base, Bedder said that in 1996, tin consumption will have grown 7,500 tonnes annually thanks to develpment programs devised by ITRI to boost demand.
In 1998, tin consumption will be 30,000 tonnes higher than in 1994, representing a slight slowdown in increase.

ITRI is largely funded by the world's tin producers. "Our work is geared to what we know to be the future increase in production," Bedder said, adding this would avoid significant surpluses or deficits.
The Institute is pinning much of its short-term hopes on usurping lead in the shotgun cartridge market - a sector where bismuth and steel are trying to muscle in too.
Bedder said toxic lead shot was facing voluntary and legal bans in several countries, while steel shot ricochets and rusts.
"In Europe there is a move to ban lead shot completely," Bedder said. Most wild birds died from lead shot poisoning after being hit.
Bismuth shot was brittle and 15 percent more expensive than tin, Bedder said.

"Commercial production of tin shot began in Europe six weeks ago and the first cartridges have been sold," Bedder said. "The potential is phenomenal. Some 120,000 tonnes a year of metal is blown in the air in the world. If we get 20 percent of that we are taking about 20,000 tonnes of tin."
But some of the U.S. tin association's members were skeptical, and said the more expensive tin shot "will never fly" unless it could be recycled in some way to make it cheaper.
However, Bedder said one U.S. shot manufacturer "was desperately keen to get involved" in tin shot.
Bedder said if all solder becomes lead-free and used only tin, annual consumption of tin would increase by 30,000 tonnes.

Products such as photocopiers and mobile phones using lead-free solder were being developed. A Canadian telephone company will start selling a lead-free telephone within three weeks. It will be eight cents cheaper than its traditionally soldered counterpart because of recycling savings, Bedder said.

Zinc stannates, or a tin and zinc chemical combination, were seeking to wrest a greater share of the fire retardant market from antimony trioxide. When stannates eventually burned, they produced only half the smoke made by burning antimony trioxide, Bedder said.

The aluminum beverage can has toppled its tinplate counterpart in some countries such as the U.S., pushing annual tin consumption in this use to under 50,000 tonnes compared to a peak of 82,000 tonnes in 1974, Bedder said.

Key markets targeted for steel beverage cans were in the U.S., Far East and developing countries. "Fillers want a shaped can, they want to mimic the bottle a little bit," Bedder said, adding that steel cans were cheaper, and more easy to shape and recycle extensively than aluminum.

But not all steel companies outside Europe could produce the high quality tinplated sheet needed for beverage cans. "There are discussions going on between U.S. and European steel companies for technology transfer," Bedder said.
Combined, ITRI's market develpoment projects look to a potential increase of 120,000 to 150,000 tonnes in annual tin consumption.
CRU International expects Western tin consumption to reach 192,500 tonnes this year.
